checks.claim: Franklin headed a royal commission on Mesmer's animal magnetism in 1784 (appointed 12 March 1784; Franklin president/titular head; Lavoisier a member)
checks.note: Wikipedia also: Franklin the 'titular head'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_Animal_Magnetism

checks.claim: Mesmer taught an unseen fluid that a healer directs into the sick, bringing on curative crises (fits)
checks.note: Grokipedia: invisible universal fluid channelled through the magnetiser's body into patients; an 'artificial crisis' of convulsions taken as the cure. Fair plain-words simplification.

checks.claim: Lavoisier planned the two trials: magnetised without knowing, and told they were magnetised when they were not
checks.note: Wikipedia: Lavoisier proposed 'magnetising people without their knowledge and ... persuading them that they are being magnetised when they are not'. James Lind Library (https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/?p=14283) quotes Lavoisier's own plan and judges him the most likely designer. (American Heritage credits Franklin; a minority view, not a reason to change.)

checks.claim: Key: the trials separated the fluid from the patients' belief (imagination)
Wrong: 'the fluid and an iron magnet's pull' (magnets were not one of the two causes tested)
checks.note: Mesmer dropped physical magnets by early 1776; the commission's two causes were fluid and imagination.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'the honest patients and the fakers'
checks.note: The design tested cause (fluid vs imagination), not honesty; the commission put the fits down to imagination, not fakery.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'the fluid up close and from far away'
Context: blindfolds and screens made these among the first blind tests on record
checks.note: JLL: 'the first known experiments using blind comparisons'; Wikipedia: first to use blindfolding; 'among the first' is safely hedged.

checks.claim: Context: Mesmer had long since given up iron magnets, saying the cure came from his fluid
checks.note: Magnets on Franziska Oesterlin in 1774; dropped by early 1776, eight years before the commission.

checks.claim: Charles d'Eslon, a physician and follower of Mesmer, let the commission test his practice (Mesmer refused)
checks.note: Grokipedia: Mesmer declined; the commission examined his associate d'Eslon, a royal physician.

checks.claim: A blindfolded woman (dame P-) was persuaded d'Eslon was magnetising her though he was not there; crisis within about three minutes
checks.note: PDR: d'Eslon 'was not even around'; crisis 'within the space of three minutes'.

checks.claim: Another woman (Mlle B-) was magnetised for half an hour from behind a paper partition without knowing, and showed no crisis
checks.note: PDR: 'a full half hour from behind a paper partition' while chatting with a commissioner. Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Royal_Commission_on_Animal_Magnetism): a patient unaware of the practitioner had no crises in about 30 minutes behind a paper frame. Optional enrichment: when the magnetiser then came out and repeated the passes in full view, she collapsed within minutes (PDR), which supports the key further.

checks.claim: Key: only the one who believed it fell into a fit; wrong choices (only the treated one, both, neither) are wrong
checks.note: The stem defines the screened woman's trial as the half hour behind the screen, so 'Both' is not defensible.

checks.claim: Context: such an effect, from expecting a treatment, is now called a placebo effect
checks.note: Worded as a modern label, not as a 1784 claim; PDR calls the sham condition 'a rudimentary placebo control condition'.

checks.claim: d'Eslon magnetised one apricot tree in Franklin's garden/orchard at Passy
checks.note: PDR: 'Deslon magnetised the tree'; an apricot tree in Franklin's orchard. American Heritage also says apricot.

checks.claim: d'Eslon brought a boy he had found sensitive to the fluid
checks.note: JLL: d'Eslon was to bring a subject already shown to be 'sensitive'; PDR: a twelve-year-old boy 'of his choosing'.

checks.claim: The boy was blindfolded and hugged trees for two minutes each; crisis at the fourth, which was not magnetised
checks.note: American Heritage: blindfolded, four trees, fainted at the fourth; PDR: two minutes each, none magnetised, crisis at the fourth; Wikipedia: fainted at one of the other (unmagnetised) trees.

checks.claim: Key: the commission put the fits down to the patients' imagination
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'touch, imagination, [and] imitation'; official summary 'imagination is everything, magnetism nothing'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: fluid spreading between trees; a fluid too faint to measure; tricks the healers taught
checks.note: The commission found no evidence of a fluid at all and did not charge the healers with coaching fakery.

checks.claim: Context: nothing proved the fluid existed; imagination helped by touch and imitation
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'touch, imagination, and imitation'.

checks.claim: Context: the report was printed in at least 20,000 copies and spread across France and beyond
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'at least 20,000 copies', widely circulated in France and neighbouring countries; Grokipedia: 'over 20,000 copies'.

checks.claim: Panel of 13 (the Hans Commission): a vet, a circus manager, a cavalry officer, several schoolteachers, the director of the Berlin zoo
September 1904 verdict: no tricks involved
checks.note: Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Clever_Hans): no intentional trickery, though it could not explain the successes; Pfungst's book dates the report 12 September 1904.

checks.claim: Carl Stumpf led the panel; Pfungst was his assistant
checks.note: Pfungst a 'volunteer assistant in the laboratory of Carl Stumpf'; Wikipedia (Clever Hans): Stumpf formed the panel.

checks.claim: Key: no one cheated, yet Hans was not counting
checks.note: Pfungst's book (1911 Rahn translation): answers right only when the questioner knew and was seen; cues involuntary.

checks.claim: Wrong: Hans really was counting; von Osten cheated; a helper signalled from the crowd
checks.note: Von Osten 'genuinely convinced'; Pfungst isolated horse and questioner from spectators and Hans still answered.

checks.claim: Context: von Osten believed in his horse, charged nothing, and Hans answered for strangers too
checks.note: 'never charged admission'; correct answers even when von Osten did not ask.

checks.claim: Von Osten, a retired mathematics teacher in Berlin
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'retired mathematics teacher'; Skeptoid: 'retired Prussian schoolmaster in Berlin'; Wikipedia: gymnasium mathematics teacher.

checks.claim: Hans was said to do sums, spell and tell the time by tapping a hoof
checks.note: Wikipedia lists add, subtract ... 'tell the time', read, spell.

checks.claim: Key: Hans failed when the questioner did not know the answer
checks.note: Pfungst's book: number cards, 8% right without the questioner's knowledge (49 tests) vs 98% with it (42 tests).

checks.claim: Wrong: a stranger questioner; von Osten out of the room (Hans still answered)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Even when von Osten stepped away, the horse continued to provide answers'; Wikipedia: correct even when von Osten did not ask.

checks.claim: Wrong: a written question (Hans still answered when the questioner knew the word)
checks.note: Skeptoid: written words right when the word was known, wrong when it was not.

checks.claim: Blinders: shields beside a horse's eyes that block the side view
Questioner seen: 50 of 56 right (89%)
checks.note: Pfungst's own book: 102 tests with large blinders; 56 'seen', 89% correct (= 50); 35 'not seen'; 11 'undecided' (18%). Wikipedia gives '89 percent (50 out of 56)'.

checks.claim: Key: questioner out of sight, 2 of 35 right
checks.note: Pfungst: '6% of Hans's answers were correct (i. e. only two)' of the 35 'not seen' cases. Wikipedia: 'six percent (2 out of 35)'.

checks.claim: Context: blinders worn in both kinds of trial; about 89% vs about 6%
checks.note: All 102 tests used the large blinders.

checks.claim: Questioners watched the hoof, tense, as the taps went on
checks.note: Wikipedia: posture and expression changed with 'an increase in tension', released at the final tap; Pfungst: the questioner 'involuntarily, bent his head and trunk slightly forward'.

checks.claim: Key: a tiny upward jerk of the head told Hans to stop
checks.note: Pfungst: 'As soon as the desired number of taps was given, the questioner would make a slight upward jerk of the head.'

checks.claim: Wrong: tongue click, foot tap, word under the breath
checks.note: The cue was visual (Hans failed when he could not see the questioner).

checks.claim: Context: about a millimetre by one account
checks.note: Grokipedia: upward jerks 'averaging 1 mm'; some as small as 1/5 mm.

checks.claim: Context: no questioner knew he was making it, so the 1904 panel found no tricks
checks.note: 'The trainer was entirely unaware that he was providing such clues.'

checks.claim: Key: after learning the cue, Pfungst as questioner still gave it without meaning to
checks.note: Pfungst, ch. III: 'even after I had discovered the nature of these movements and had thus become enabled to call forth at will all the various responses ... I still succeeded in giving the signs in the earlier naive involuntary manner.' Grokipedia: he found himself 'unwittingly providing similar cues'.

checks.claim: Wrong: he held still so Hans could not answer; he held still yet Hans answered; Hans read only von Osten's cues
checks.note: Hans answered Pfungst and strangers, so 'only von Osten' is wrong; the book reports no trial in which Pfungst held still. (He could produce answers at will, but that is not one of the choices.)

checks.claim: Context: a questioner cannot simply decide not to give a cue
checks.note: Pfungst, ch. IV: those 'initiated into the secret' found it very difficult, sometimes almost impossible, to hold back the movements on purpose. 'Cannot simply decide' is a fair plain-words version.

checks.claim: Context: now called the Clever Hans effect; experiments are built to avoid it
checks.note: 'has had a large effect on experimental design and methodology'.

checks.claim: Emily Rosa was nine at her first trials, 1996, for a (4th-grade) science fair
checks.note: JAMA: 'The first series of tests was conducted when she was 9 years old'; Grokipedia and Wikipedia: fourth-grade science fair. (Born 6 Feb 1987; JAMA paper 1 April 1998, age 11.)

checks.claim: Set-up: hands through cutouts at the base of a tall screen; coin toss picked the hand; she hovered her hand over it; practitioner named which
checks.note: 'a tall, opaque screen with cutouts at its base'; 'flipped a coin'; hand 8 to 10 cm above the target.

checks.claim: 'Human energy field' given as the practitioners' term
checks.note: Abstract: a 'human energy field' perceptible above the skin. Attributed fairly; no mockery.

checks.claim: 280 trials over 1996 and 1997, 21 practitioners, 123 right (44%)
checks.note: 15 in 1996, 13 in 1997 including 7 repeats = 21; 123 of 280.

checks.claim: Key: no sense of her field, only guessing; wrong: weak sense, sense reversed, sense dulled by the screen
checks.note: JAMA: 'close to what would be expected for random chance'; the authors concluded the claims groundless.

checks.claim: Context: guessing gives about 140 of 280; true ability should be 100%
checks.note: 'A score of 50% would be expected through chance alone'; should locate the hand '100% of the time'.

checks.claim: Context: 123 'is within the range that guessing gives'
checks.note: Wikipedia says 'lower than, though within the range of, mere chance', but the arithmetic is borderline: for pure guessing on 280 coin-toss targets, P(123 or fewer) = 0.024 (two-sided about 0.048), and the central 95% band for guessing is 124 to 156, so 123 sits just outside it. A maths-minded reader can call this wrong. Fix: use the paper's own words, e.g. 'The practitioners' 123, or 44 percent, is close to what guessing gives, the paper's authors said, and far below the every-time score a real sense should give; a score a little under half is chance at work, not a sense working backward.'

checks.claim: Pass mark set in advance: at least 8 of 10
checks.note: 'We decided in advance that an individual would pass by making 8 or more correct selections'; group mean had to exceed 6.7.

checks.claim: Guessing gives about 5 of 10
checks.note: 50% by chance.

checks.claim: Key: so the mark cannot shift after the results
checks.note: Fixing decision rules before data guards against changing the claim after the results are known.

checks.claim: Wrong: luck can never earn a pass (it can: about 1 in 18); people cannot cheat (that is the screen's job); stop when one passes
checks.note: Computed: P(8 or more of 10 by guessing) = 56/1024 = 0.055, about 1 in 18.

checks.claim: Context: guessing reaches 8 of 10 about once in 18 tries; scientists now post plans before gathering data
checks.note: Arithmetic checked (1024/56 = 18.3).

unit_notes: Fairness: no wording mocks Mesmer, d'Eslon, von Osten or the therapeutic touch practitioners; von Osten is shown as honest, the fits as real, the energy field as the practitioners' own term. Clever Hans figures were checked against Pfungst's own 1911 English text (Utrecht University OCR copy): 102 blinder tests, 56 seen at 89% (50), 35 not seen at 6% ('only two'), 11 undecided; blinders worn throughout. Only flag: the Rosa context's 'within the range that guessing gives', borderline by exact binomial arithmetic (123 is just below the 95% band 124-156); reword to the paper's 'close to chance'. Optional: in the paper-screen trial, Mlle B- collapsed within minutes once the magnetiser stepped out and repeated the passes in full view (PDR), which could enrich that context.
